title: The Most Misunderstood Job on Earth: Flight Attendant

voice_performance.performance_intent: A calm, warm female narrator who sounds like a trusted crew member sharing a surprising secret, with a small smile in the comic reversals and firm precision on safety facts.
voice_performance.energy_curve: Immediate amused reversal, purposeful lift through training, deliberate focus on the 90-second fact, intimate curiosity at the door greeting, then a warm confident close.
voice_performance.pause_policy: Use short breaths after object transformations, a full half-beat before 'ninety seconds,' and a clear pause before the final reframe and next-episode line.

provider_notes.captioning: Word-level captions mirror narration in two-to-five-word clusters; designed labels show only facts or punch words so they do not duplicate whole sentences.

sections.label: Act one — training
sections.text: The FAA says their main duty is keeping passengers safe. Before the snack cart, there are weeks of drills: evacuation slides, emergency exits, firefighting, first aid, and medical response.
sections.speaker_directions: Authoritative but buoyant; turn the training list into a rhythmic build.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: Keep the list even and clear, with tiny breaths between visual swaps.
delivery_cues.provider_text: The F A A says their main duty is keeping passengers safe. <break time="250ms"/> Before the snack cart, there are weeks of drills: evacuation slides, emergency exits, firefighting, first aid, and medical response.

enhancement_cues.description: Training scrapbook flips through slide, exit, fire, first-aid, and AED cut-outs.

sections.label: Act two — 90 seconds
sections.text: Here is why speed matters. For aircraft with more than forty-four passenger seats, certification rules require a full-capacity evacuation demonstration in ninety seconds, under simulated emergency conditions. That is a test standard, not a promise for every real accident.
sections.speaker_directions: Slow slightly for the number and the legal caveat; sound precise, not ominous.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: Give 'ninety seconds' a clean half-beat of space; soften into the corrective caveat.
delivery_cues.provider_text: Here is why speed matters. <break time="350ms"/> For aircraft with more than forty-four passenger seats, certification rules require a full-capacity evacuation demonstration in <emphasis level="moderate">ninety seconds</emphasis>, under simulated emergency conditions. <break time="300ms"/> That is a test standard, not a promise for every real accident.

enhancement_cues.description: Hero paper timer reads 90 SECONDS with small CERTIFICATION TEST label.
Overhead cabin aisle empties into two paper exit arrows.

sections.label: Act three — the greeting
sections.text: And that friendly hello at the door? It is also an early safety check: who may need help, who seems unwell or intoxicated, and whether exit-row passengers can perform emergency tasks.
sections.speaker_directions: Return to an intimate, lightly conspiratorial tone without implying invasive profiling.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: Treat each observation as assistance and readiness, not suspicion.
delivery_cues.provider_text: And that friendly hello at the door? <break time="220ms"/> It is also an early safety check: who may need help, who seems unwell or intoxicated, and whether exit-row passengers can perform emergency tasks.

enhancement_cues.description: Doorway greeting becomes three gentle paper thought-bubbles: assistance, wellness, exit-row readiness.

sections.label: Act three — the pay clock
sections.text: One more surprise: in many traditional pay systems, the main hourly clock starts when the aircraft door closes, even though boarding work starts earlier. Newer contracts increasingly add boarding pay, so rules vary by airline.
sections.speaker_directions: Matter-of-fact, sympathetic, and careful with the current caveat.
